name: Sinus Infection (Sinusitis)
prevalence: About 29 million U.S. adults each year
overview: A sinus infection happens when the moist air spaces behind your cheeks, nose, and forehead get inflamed and filled with mucus, usually after a cold. That causes facial pressure, stuffiness, and thick drainage. Most cases are caused by viruses and clear up on their own within a week or two — antibiotics only help when bacteria are to blame. Rest, fluids, saline rinses, and time are often the best medicine.
symptoms: Pressure or pain around the cheeks, eyes, or forehead

drugs.name: Saline nasal rinse
drugs.note: Flushes out mucus and soothes irritated sinuses.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) / Ibuprofen (Advil)
drugs.note: Eases facial pain, pressure, and fever.

drugs.name: Fluticasone (Flonase)
drugs.note: Calms swelling inside the nose.

drugs.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
drugs.note: Short-term relief for a stuffed-up nose.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin)
drugs.note: For bacterial infections that aren't improving on their own.

redFlags: Swelling or redness around an eye, vision changes, severe headache with a stiff neck, or confusion can mean the infection is spreading — go to the ER.

name: Ear Infections
prevalence: About 5 out of 6 children have one by age 3
overview: Ear infections happen when fluid builds up behind the eardrum and gets infected, usually during or after a cold. They're one of the most common reasons young children see a doctor, though adults get them too. The classic signs are ear pain, fussiness, and trouble hearing. Many mild cases clear up on their own within a few days; antibiotics help when symptoms are severe or don't improve.
symptoms: Ear pain, or tugging at the ear in young kids

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: First step for easing ear pain and fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another good option for pain and fever.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.note: The usual first choice when an antibiotic is needed.

drugs.name: Ear tubes (tympanostomy)
drugs.note: A minor surgery for kids who get infection after infection.

redFlags: A high fever with a stiff neck, swelling or redness behind the ear, or a child who is unusually drowsy or hard to wake needs emergency care.

name: Tinnitus (Ringing in the Ears)
overview: Tinnitus is hearing a sound — ringing, buzzing, or hissing — that isn't coming from the outside world. It's usually linked to age-related hearing loss, loud-noise exposure, or even earwax buildup, and it's rarely a sign of something dangerous. There's no single cure, but many people find real relief with hearing aids, sound machines, and counseling approaches that teach the brain to tune the noise out.
symptoms: Ringing, buzzing, hissing, or humming in the ears
Sound seems louder in quiet places, especially at night
Often comes along with some hearing loss
May be constant or come and go

drugs.name: Hearing aids
drugs.note: Boosting outside sound often makes the ringing fade into the background.

drugs.name: Sound therapy (white-noise machines)
drugs.note: Masks the ringing, especially at bedtime.

drugs.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
drugs.note: Teaches the brain to react less to the sound.

drugs.name: Earwax removal
drugs.note: A quick fix when built-up wax is the cause.

redFlags: Tinnitus in only one ear, tinnitus that pulses with your heartbeat, or ringing with sudden hearing loss needs prompt evaluation — sudden hearing loss is a same-day emergency.

name: Hearing Loss
prevalence: About 1 in 8 Americans age 12 and older
overview: Hearing loss usually creeps in slowly, most often from aging, years of loud noise, or both. You might find yourself asking people to repeat things or turning the TV up. It matters because untreated hearing loss can lead to isolation and strain relationships, but today's options — including hearing aids sold over the counter — are better and easier to get than ever. A simple hearing test is the place to start.
symptoms: Trouble following conversations in noisy places
Turning the TV or phone volume way up

drugs.name: Hearing aids
drugs.note: The main treatment — now sold over the counter for mild-to-moderate loss.

drugs.name: Earwax removal
drugs.note: A quick fix when wax buildup is the culprit.

drugs.name: Assistive listening devices
drugs.note: Phone captions and TV streamers fill in the gaps.

drugs.name: Cochlear implant
drugs.note: For severe loss when hearing aids aren't enough.

redFlags: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears is a medical emergency — seek care the same day, because quick treatment can sometimes save your hearing.

name: Vertigo (BPPV)
prevalence: About 2 in 100 adults at some point
overview: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo — that sudden spinning feeling. It happens when tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear drift out of place, confusing your balance sensors whenever you roll over in bed or tilt your head. The spells are brief but can be intense. The good news: a simple series of head movements called the Epley maneuver fixes most cases, often in a single office visit.
symptoms: Brief spinning sensation triggered by head movements
Worse when rolling over in bed or looking up
Episodes usually last less than a minute

drugs.name: Epley maneuver
drugs.note: Guided head movements that put the loose crystals back in place — the main treatment.

drugs.name: Meclizine (Antivert)
drugs.note: Short-term help for the dizzy, queasy feeling.

drugs.name: Vestibular rehab exercises
drugs.note: Retrains your balance system if symptoms linger.

drugs.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
drugs.note: For severe nausea during bad spells.

redFlags: Vertigo with double vision, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, or a sudden severe headache could be a stroke — call 911.

name: Tonsillitis
prevalence: Millions of U.S. cases a year, mostly kids ages 5–15
overview: Tonsillitis means the tonsils — the two soft pads at the back of the throat — are inflamed, usually from a virus and sometimes from strep bacteria. It brings a sore throat, trouble swallowing, fever, and swollen glands. Viral cases get better with rest and fluids; strep needs antibiotics. Tonsil-removal surgery is reserved these days for kids and adults who get infections again and again.
symptoms: Sore throat and pain when swallowing
Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches
Swollen, tender glands in the neck

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases throat pain and fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another solid choice for pain and fever.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin / Penicillin
drugs.note: First choice when a strep test comes back positive.

drugs.name: Tonsillectomy
drugs.note: Surgery to remove the tonsils after frequent repeat infections.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, drooling, inability to swallow, a muffled voice, or severe one-sided throat swelling can signal a serious abscess — go to the ER.

name: Laryngitis
prevalence: Very common — about 1 in 3 people have a voice problem at some point
overview: Laryngitis is irritation of the voice box (larynx) that leaves you hoarse, raspy, or barely able to speak above a whisper. Most cases come from a cold virus or from overusing your voice — think cheering at a game — and they heal on their own within a week or two. Resting your voice and drinking plenty of fluids speeds things along; antibiotics almost never help. Hoarseness that drags on for weeks deserves a checkup.
symptoms: Tickling or raw feeling in the throat

drugs.name: Voice rest and fluids
drugs.note: The main treatment — give the vocal cords time to heal.

drugs.name: Humidifier or steam
drugs.note: Moist air soothes an irritated voice box.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) / Ibuprofen (Advil)
drugs.note: Eases throat soreness.

drugs.name: Omeprazole (Prilosec)
drugs.note: Helps when stomach acid reflux is behind chronic hoarseness.

redFlags: Hoarseness with trouble breathing, noisy breathing, or trouble swallowing needs ER care right away; hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs a doctor's look.
